subject: Performance alignment: p95/p99 gating, streaming concurrency, and canary criteria
messages:
From: Claire Zhou <claire.zhou@veridian.ai>
To: Lukas Meyer <lukas_meyer@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 5 Nov 2026 14:12:00 -0800
Subject: Thanks for the demo — clarifying latency targets

Thanks again for the demo earlier today. A few follow-up items from our side so we can align on an executable canary: 

- Quick context: our production traffic is very spiky on inference start (chat open token bursts) and we multiplex long-running streaming sessions (avg session 42s). Current provider (incumbent.ai) reports typical numbers: p95 ~= 180ms, p99 ~= 700ms for short queries (<= 64 tokens) but streaming tails stretch depending on concurrency.
- Veridian target goals for migration: p95 end-to-end <= 120ms for short queries, p99 end-to-end <= 450ms; sustained streaming concurrency target ~200 simultaneous sessions; burst concurrency up to 600 for <5m windows.

What we need from Redwood to feel comfortable moving forward:
1) A recommended canary plan with pass/fail gating for p95/p99 and streaming concurrency.
2) Specific measurement points (client-to-client E2E path we should instrument) and recommended sampling windows.
3) Any known limitations with streaming + concurrency that would cause a fallback to the incumbent (e.g., connection limits, per-VM session memory pressure).

Attaching a small CSV with our traffic histogram and a placeholder KPI sheet. Happy to do a 30–45m runbook call tomorrow.

Thanks,
Claire
Senior Platform Engineer, Veridian AI
ops@veridian.ai

From: Lukas Meyer To: Claire Zhou Cc: Ben Carter , Laura Bennett Date: Thu, 5 Nov 2026 18:05:00 -0800 Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — clarifying latency targets Claire — thanks for the clear targets and the histograms, very helpful. Quick recap and a concrete canary proposal from our side so we have a single source of truth: Recap of Veridian targets (from your note): - p95 E2E (short queries <=64 tokens): target <= 120ms - p99 E2E (short queries <=64 tokens): target <= 450ms - Sustained streaming concurrency: 200 sessions - Burst concurrency: up to 600 sessions (short windows)
Our hosted plan recommendations and gating logic: 1) Baseline acceptance windows - Warm baseline run (no cold starts): 1-hour steady-state at 200 sustained sessions; success if p95 <=120ms AND p99 <=450ms for short queries; streaming sessions must maintain <15% frame-drop or buffer refill events. 2) Burst stress run - 30-minute burst window that ramps 200 -> 600 concurrent sessions over 5 minutes and sustains 600 for 10 minutes, followed by 15 minutes decay. Success if p95 <=200ms AND p99 <=900ms (burst tolerance) and no more than 5% of sessions experience connection resets attributable to the inference layer. 3) Canary rollout acceptance (end-to-end) - Canary passes if both baseline and burst runs meet gating AND production-weighted errors (4xx/5xx attributed to inference) are not increased by >0.5 percentage points vs incumbent in the same windows. Instrumentation & measurement notes: - Instrumentation points we recommend you enable: client request timestamp, proxy ingress, redwood edge ingress, model service ingress/egress, response assembled timestamp. We will provide a small SDK snippet that maps our headers to your traces so measurements are truly E2E. - Sampling: full sampling for the 1-hour baseline; 10% sampling for ongoing health checks once canary is in traffic. Known constraints and mitigations: - Streaming concurrency: our hosted runtime supports 1,200 concurrent streaming sessions per region on standard nodes, but per-tenant session memory and KV cache can impact p99 under very bursty small-token patterns. Mitigation: pre-warm KV cache for common prefixes and enforce short keepalive thresholds during the burst to avoid resource hoarding. - Fallbacks: we will configure a fast-fail policy that routes overflow traffic to a pinned model variant with lower resource intensity (quantized) while keeping the same API. This will trade slight quality for latency stability. Next steps proposed: - I will upload a draft canary-run workbook (canary_plan_kpis.xlsx) with exact measurement columns and thresholds. - Schedule a runbook call: tomorrow 10:00–10:45 PT? Ben will own the run and Laura will coordinate access. Ben/Laura — any additions? Best, Lukas Meyer Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Date: Fri, 6 Nov 2026 08:23:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — clarifying latency targets

Claire — quick notes on concurrency tuning and streaming buffering (piggybacking on Lukas):

- We suggest a small per-client concurrency cap (90–120) for initial canary to avoid head-of-line effects and allow fair multiplexing across sessions. This can be relaxed once warmed.
- Streaming buffer strategy: use a 150–300ms writable buffer on the client side; Redwood's server-side buffer management aims to deliver frames within 50ms of generation for short tokens in steady state.
- For the burst run, we'll instrument per-VM session counts and trigger autoscale at 70% utilization with a 60s cooldown to avoid oscillation.

I added a few inline comments to the attached workbook (canary_plan_kpis.xlsx). If that looks good we can lock the runbook and I’ll fire the first dry-run (no traffic shift) at the time you confirm.

—Ben
Ben Carter
